explain.say: Almost every precise metal part, from a bicycle axle to a jet engine shaft, is finished by machining: cutting away chips with a hard tool. Look at the lathe. The motor spins the chuck and the workpiece, a 50 millimetre steel bar, while the cutting tool slides along and peels off a chip.

explain.say: Now the real thing in 3D: a lathe. The chuck spins the workpiece, and the cutting tool on the carriage peels off a thin ribbon of metal. That is turning. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.

explain.say: The key number is cutting speed: how fast the surface passes the tool. A carbide tool on mild steel likes about 150 metres per minute. Speed equals pi D N, so the spindle speed N is 1000 times 150 over pi times 50: about 955 rpm. What happens to N for a thinner bar?

explain.say: It must spin faster to keep the same surface speed. Now how much metal comes off: the material removal rate is cutting speed times feed times depth of cut. With 0.2 millimetres per revolution and a 2 millimetre cut, that is 60 cubic centimetres per minute. The cutting force is about 800 newtons, so the power is 800 times 2.5 metres per second, 2 kilowatts.

explain.say: Turning is just one process. See the groups? In milling a toothed cutter spins and the work moves under it, making flat faces and slots. In drilling the drill spins and feeds into the work. Same rules: cutting speed sets the spindle speed. Which process would make a flat face on a block?

draw.text: Milling and drilling: the tool spins; the work is held still or fed

explain.say: Milling! One last trade-off. Cut faster and the tool wears out sooner. Taylor found that V times T to the n is constant. With n 0.25 and C 400, a tool lasts 51 minutes at 150 metres per minute but only 16 at 200. See the steep curve? Superb work. Exam tip: mind the 1000 when converting metres to millimetres.

faq.q: What does the chuck do on a lathe?
faq.a: The chuck grips the workpiece and spins it with the spindle, so the tool can cut a round shape as it feeds along.

faq.q: How do I calculate spindle speed for turning?
faq.a: N equals 1000 times the cutting speed in metres per minute divided by pi times the diameter in millimetres. For 150 metres per minute on a 50 millimetre bar, that is about 955 rpm.
asks: what does the cutting tool do

faq.q: What is Taylor's tool life equation?
faq.a: V times T to the power n equals C, where V is cutting speed, T tool life, and n and C depend on the tool and work materials. For carbide, n is often about 0.25.

faq.q: What is the difference between turning and milling?
faq.a: In turning the workpiece spins and a single-point tool feeds along it, making round parts. In milling a multi-tooth cutter spins and the workpiece moves, making flat faces, slots and pockets.
The volume of metal cut away per minute: cutting speed times feed times depth of cut. Cutting power is roughly the removal rate times the specific cutting energy of the material.

facts: Cutting speed V = πDN; with D in mm and V in m/min, N = 1000V/(πD).
F. W. Taylor published his tool life equation in 1907.
